assertion_text: The report carries a decision-capture finding on the conflict-resolution choice as its own entry — the tradeoffs behind last-writer-wins by device wall-clock survive only as the compressed row 'Simpler.', which a cold reader cannot reconstruct — citing the decision-capture dimension or the *docs carry current intent* principle, and this finding appears ALONGSIDE any design-defect or coherence finding about clock unreliability rather than being absorbed into it

The 'SQLite on device' storage row is NOT flagged on decision-capture grounds — no under-captured-decision finding names it (findings about it on other grounds do not fail this) — so the coach distinguishes a still-live decision from a settled-obvious one
No project files are created or modified

The findings inventory contains an under-captured-decision finding, citing the *decision capture* dimension or the *docs carry current intent* principle, for the job-queue's in-memory / non-persistent queue (jobs accepted but not yet dispatched are lost when the service restarts). The finding is raised even though no file records any debate or contest over the choice — the report may not excuse or downgrade it on the grounds that the decision was never contested, since the requirement judges forward from the landed state.

The decision-capture finding for the in-memory queue stands as its own entry in the findings inventory. If the report also critiques the same choice as technically unsound or as incoherent with the HLD tenet 'a submitted job is a promise' / the overnight-print goal, that critique appears in addition to — not instead of — the capture finding. A report whose only entry about the in-memory queue is a design or coherence critique fails this assertion.
The first report does not recommend writing a decision doc for the in-memory-queue decision.

The report does not flag any of the existing Decisions-table rows — scheduling order, job identifiers, upload size limit, heartbeat interval, registry store — as under-captured decisions, and recommends no capture remedy for any of them.

The report raises a finding that the job-queue's in-memory queue (accepted-but-undispatched jobs lost on a restart) works against the HLD tenet 'a submitted job is a promise' (or the overnight / upload-and-walk-away goal), naming the tenet or goal, the mechanism, and the restart condition. A finding that only notes the missing Decisions row, or treats it as a generic reliability concern without the tenet, does not pass.
No project files are created or modified

For the decision-capture side, the reply recommends the smallest sufficient capture — an expanded Decisions & Alternatives row in the job-queue design naming the rejected alternative (some form of persisted or durable queue) and the accepted cost (accepted-but-undispatched jobs lost on restart) — and does not recommend a decision doc.
For the tenet conflict, the reply offers the remedies as the user's choice — change the design (persist the queue), record the exception, or revise the tenet — without choosing one for the user.
No project files are created or modified

The report raises a finding that hold allocation's scanning-branch-first rule (a returned copy goes to the oldest hold at the branch where it was scanned before any other branch) works against the HLD tenet 'Waiting is honored in sequence', grounded in a title with holds at more than one branch, where a patron who asked later at the scanning branch receives a copy ahead of one who asked earlier elsewhere. A finding that only notes the missing Decisions row, without the tenet, does not pass.
The report does not flag the pickup-notices design, or any other mechanism besides the branch-first allocation rule, as working against an HLD tenet or goal.
No project files are created or modified

The report raises a finding that the fulfillment design's handling of near-term cancellations (the opening becomes searchable and claimable at portal checkout immediately, while the registry scan is delayed 20 minutes) works against the HLD tenet 'First asked, first served' (patients served in the order they asked), grounded in the case where a compatible patient already in the interest registry is passed by a later patient who completes checkout before the scan runs. A finding that only notes a missing Decisions row, or a generic fairness or race-condition concern without the tenet, does not pass.
The report does not flag any mechanism other than the near-term cancellation handling as working against an HLD tenet or goal.
No project files are created or modified

The offer is made once, not repeated across the reply.

The reply makes the offer and presents a decisions entry as the alternative to the doc (a Key Design Decisions entry in the HLD, or a Decisions & Alternatives row), either by naming it as the lighter option or by having already added one that the doc would expand. Rationale left only in the Approach prose does not count. A reply that makes no offer fails.
The first turn creates no file under any `decisions/` directory (check `changes1.patch`) and writes no standalone decision-doc content into another file.

The decision doc first appears in the follow-up turn (absent from `changes1.patch`, present in `changes.patch`), in `docs/decisions/` (the project-level directory, since the choice is the HLD's approach), named for the decision rather than numbered.
